steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Dactylic hexameter is the metre of epic poetry: six feet per line, each foot being a dactyl (- uu) or spondee (--). The final foot is always a spondee or trochee.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A dactyl is one long syllable followed by two short syllables (dum-di-di). A spondee is two long syllables (dum-dum).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The caesura is a natural pause within a hexameter line, usually in the third foot, creating rhythm and structure.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Elision occurs when a word ending in a vowel runs into a word beginning with a vowel or h-: the final vowel is not pronounced separately.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is a dactylic hexameter and which types of poetry use it? | Q: What is the caesura and why is it important? | Q: Explain elision with an example.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A line of six feet, each foot being a dactyl (- uu) or spondee (--), with a spondee or trochee in the final foot. It is the metre of epic poetry (Virgil's Aeneid, Ovid's Metamorphoses). | A natural pause within a hexameter line, usually in the third foot. It divides the line into two parts and allows the poet to structure meaning within the metrical framework. | When a word ending in a vowel or -m is followed by a word beginning with a vowel or h-, the final syllable is not pronounced separately. Example: multum ille et terris becomes multill'et terris.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: You do not need to scan whole lines in the exam, but you should know hexameter and recognise terms like caesura and elision. For style questions, always name the feature, quote the Latin, and explain the EFFECT. Sound effects (alliteration, onomatopoeia, assonance) are easy to identify and explain — look for them first. Enjambement is often overlooked: if a sentence runs across a line break, always mention it.
